title: The cook's instructions
hook: Dogen's instructions for the cook: treat rice and water as your own eyes

segments.voice: This week walked through a Zen hall: the teacher's room, the slow walk, the bowls, the broom, the board, the chant. Yesterday's line: chanting zen. Did your whole attention go into one sound? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine, and the week closes in the kitchen.

Midday, blazing sun, stone pavement too hot to stand on. An old monk with no hat, a bamboo staff in his hand, is spreading mushrooms out to dry, sweat pouring off him. A young visitor from Japan, Dogen, stops and asks him: why are you doing this yourself? Why not let a helper do it? The old cook answers, in paraphrase: others are not me. Dogen tries again: then why now, in this heat? The answer: if not now, when? Dogen tells this story in a short text he wrote for monastery cooks. Today: the cook's instructions.
screen: `AN OLD COOK IN THE NOON SUN.` → `OTHERS ARE NOT ME.` → `IF NOT NOW, WHEN?`

segments.voice: First, the job. In a Zen monastery, the head cook, the tenzo, is a senior post, given to someone whose practice is trusted. Dogen's instructions for the tenzo treat the kitchen as a meditation hall. Planning the meals, washing the rice, tending the fire: none of it is beneath anyone, and none of it is separate from the way. Second, the eyes. Dogen tells the cook, in paraphrase, to look after the rice and the water as carefully as your own eyes. Think how you treat your eyes: gently, never carelessly, never roughly. That's the care he asks for a pot of rice. He also tells the cook, in paraphrase, to look for sand while washing the rice, and for rice while throwing out the sand, so that not one grain is lost and not one stone gets through. Third, no fancy or plain food in the heart of the cook. Dogen says, in paraphrase, that a simple broth made with care is no lower than a rich dish, and a rich dish is no higher. The cook doesn't save full attention for the special meal. Every pot gets the same eyes. Fourth, the old cook in the sun. He turned down the easy way out twice. Not someone else. Not later. Dogen writes that he had nothing more to say, and walked away seeing how much the cook's work matters. The way was in this too: the mushrooms, the heat, done by your own hands, now. For anyone who has ever stood at a stove at the end of a long day, that's a striking thought: the pot of pasta is not in the way of a deeper life.
screen: `THE KITCHEN IS A MEDITATION HALL.` · `RICE AND WATER, LIKE YOUR EYES.` · `NO PLAIN DISH, NO FANCY DISH.` · `NOT SOMEONE ELSE. NOT LATER.` · then, large: `AS YOUR OWN EYES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and breathe. Bring to mind the next thing you'll cook or prepare, even if it's toast or a cup of tea. Picture your hands doing it: the water running, the bread, the knife. Now picture doing it the tenzo's way, as carefully as you'd handle your own eyes. No hurry. Nothing beneath you. Notice what changes in the picture. Then let it go and rest in the breath until the bell. The bell holds the time.
The cook's instructions. Dogen's teaching for the monastery cook: treat the rice and water as your own eyes, and cook every meal as practice. Today's word.
Your line: as your own eyes. Today, cook or prepare one thing with that care, yourself, now, and let it be as good as you can make it. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: In Soto Zen monasteries the head cook (tenzo) is a senior role, and Dogen's Instructions for the Cook (Tenzo Kyokun) is still read as a guide to treating kitchen work, and daily work in general, as practice.

what a scholar hears: the text sets encounters with old Chinese cooks at its center, and after this one Dogen says he saw how important the cook's post is.

notes: Week-end review (day 1239 = week close) looks back at days 1233–1238.

All Tenzo Kyokun material paraphrased: rice and water 'as your own eyes'; looking for sand when washing rice and for rice when discarding sand; no lower/higher between a plain broth and a rich dish; the old tenzo drying mushrooms in the sun ('others are not me', 'if not now, when'). Confirm each paraphrase against a standard translation.
Details of the mushroom scene (no hat, staff, hot pavement) follow the usual retellings of the text; confirm. Ages, dates and the monastery name deliberately omitted.
'Dogen writes that the meeting changed how he understood practice': confirm this is fair to the text.
The tenzo as a senior post: confirm.
